sections.h2: What does the Lafayette Parish Clerk of Court do with a deed?
sections.html:
The clerk records the deed, which is how a Louisiana property sale becomes effective against everyone outside the contract. Under Civil Code article 3338, a written instrument that transfers an immovable has no effect as to a third person until it is recorded in the conveyance records.

Lafayette Parish's clerk, Louis J. Perret, serves the 15th Judicial District and acts as the ex-officio recorder. The Recording Department files conveyance, mortgage and UCC documents deposited in the parish. When a document is presented, it receives an entry number with the date, hour and minute of filing, and a short description and the first parties appear on the clerk's online records search right away.

The clerk reports that about two to three hundred documents are filed each day, and that full indexing with all party names is complete by the following day.

sections.h2: What are the recording fees for a Lafayette Parish deed?
sections.html:
A conveyance or mortgage of one to five pages costs $105 to record in a single index type. The clerk's schedule includes the $5 statewide portal fee, up to ten names indexed and one certified copy in each price.

Document lengthOne book (conveyance or mortgage)Both books
1 to 5 pages$105$205
6 to 25 pages$205$405
26 to 50 pages$305$605
51 pages or more$305 plus $5 per extra page$605 plus $5 per extra page

The two-book column applies when one document goes into both records, and the fees are assessed separately for each book, except for the single $5 portal charge. The schedule also lists $5 for each name after the tenth, $20 per page for paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches, and $25 per debtor on a judgment with no Social Security or tax ID number.

sections.h2: Is there a new recording charge coming in 2027?
sections.html:
Yes. The clerk's fee page announces that, effective January 1, 2027, Act 446 of the 2026 Regular Legislative Session adds $5 to every recorded document. A closing set for late December 2026 and one set for early January 2027 can therefore carry different recording totals.

The existing $5 portal fee dates from Act 173 of 2017, effective August 1, 2018. It funds the Louisiana Clerks Remote Access Authority, a state entity that runs a statewide portal for remote access to parish land records. Both charges are in addition to the page-based fee, so ask the closing office for the total before the closing date.

sections.h2: What other charges might appear at a Lafayette Parish closing?
sections.html:
Several smaller line items show up around the main recording fee, and the clerk's schedule lists them plainly.

  • Cancellation or partial release of a single mortgage, lien or privilege: $55.
  • Cancellation with the original paraphed note: $15.
  • Real estate mortgage certificate: $20 for the first name, $10 for each additional name, and $15 for each additional property.
  • Non-lien certificate: $20 per name.
  • Copies: $1 per page in the office, $10 plus the copy fee for a certified copy, and $5 plus the copy fee for a conformed copy.

A mortgage certificate lists the recorded mortgages and privileges that stand against a seller's name. Title agents order it to confirm that every lien is paid and cancelled before the buyer's money is released.

sections.h2: How are documents prepared and submitted in Lafayette Parish?
sections.html:
The clerk wants every document to carry a caption identifying the type of act on its first page, with a 2 inch margin at the top and 1 inch at the bottom and sides, and type no smaller than 8 point. Paper can be 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches, and the clerk cites R.S. 13:844(B) for these rules.

A single document counts as all the pages presented together, including exhibits, riders, powers of attorney, property descriptions, tax certificates, surveys and mortgage certificates. That matters for the price, because the page count determines the tier.

Electronic recording is encouraged. The clerk's home page links three e-recording platforms, CSC, ePN and Simplifile, and most title companies already use one of them. If you mail a paper act, enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope or the postage is charged at actual cost.

sections.h2: Does the clerk return original documents?
sections.html:
No. The clerk states that, unlike most other states, original documents sent to the Clerk of the District Court and Ex-Officio Recorder are not returned. They become part of the parish archives.

What a filer can get back is a certified copy. It can be requested at the time of filing from the Recording Department, or later from the Land Records and Copy Department. A seller who needs proof of the sale for the Assessor or a lender should order that copy during closing.

Cancellations follow a separate path. They go first to the Cancellation Clerk in the Recording Department for verification, and in Lafayette Parish they must be in authentic form, executed before a notary public and signed by the affiant. UCC terminations use a Louisiana-approved form and can be sent directly.

sections.h2: How can you search Lafayette Parish land records?
sections.html:
The clerk's online records search covers mortgage, conveyance and UCC records, and the free eClerks LA portal indexes land, civil, marriage and probate records across Louisiana. A free alert service on eClerks LA monitors land records across parishes.

Paid land records access, including document images, is sold as a subscription: $20 for one day, $50 for 30 days or $600 for 365 days, with a $1 per page printing fee. Searching the index for liens under a seller's name before listing can show a forgotten mortgage or judgment that would otherwise appear at closing.

The clerk's home page notes that filings may become public record under the Public Records Act, and it lists items prohibited in the courthouse, including cellphones, cameras and recording devices. Bring paper documents and a printed list of the numbers you need rather than relying on a phone.

You can reach the clerk at 800 S. Buchanan St., Lafayette, LA 70501, or by mail at P.O. Box 2009, Lafayette, LA 70502. The main number is (337) 291-6400, and the Recording Department is at (337) 291-6310.

sections.h2: What should a seller confirm before the deed is recorded?
sections.html:
Confirm that property taxes are paid, because Louisiana lets any party to a conveyance of real property outside New Orleans obtain a certificate showing whether state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes have been paid, other than those for the year of the sale (R.S. 9:2901).

  • Ask for the tax certificate and for a mortgage certificate on every owner's name.
  • Check that any prior mortgage has a cancellation ready to record.
  • Ask the closing office whether the recording date falls before or after January 1, 2027.
  • Request a certified copy of the recorded act for your own file.

A seller who plans to take a cash offer should review the same list, since the buyer's title agent will run these searches before funding. Surprises are easier to fix before the closing day than after.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Lafayette Parish?
faqs.a: A one to five page conveyance in a single book costs $105, which includes a $5 portal fee, ten indexed names and one certified copy. Six to 25 pages costs $205.

faqs.q: Is there a transfer tax charge on the Lafayette Parish fee schedule?
faqs.a: The fee schedule we opened lists recording, cancellation, copy and certificate fees but no transfer tax line. Ask your closing agent for the full settlement figures.

faqs.q: Does the Lafayette Parish clerk return my original deed?
faqs.a: No. Originals become part of the parish archives. You can obtain a certified copy at filing or later from the Land Records and Copy Department.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a deed in Lafayette Parish?
faqs.a: Yes, and the clerk encourages it. The clerk's site links to CSC, ePN and Simplifile for electronic recording of mortgage, conveyance and UCC documents.
Act 446 of the 2026 Regular Legislative Session adds $5 to every recorded document starting that date, according to the clerk's fee page.
